Kuvitus: koulun fysiikan laboratorion pö: Illustration: a table in a school physics laboratory. On the left is a shield built of lead bricks, with a small radiation source in its side. Violet and blue particles and orange wavy lines leave the source towards the right. In their way are three plates in a holder: paper, aluminium and lead; the violet particles stop at the paper, the blue ones at the aluminium, and the orange waves continue. On the right a Geiger–Müller tube is fixed to a stand, its cable leads to a counter, and the counter's display shows spikes representing pulses.
Fotonin energia logaritmisella asteikoll: Photon energy on a logarithmic scale from one hundredth of an electronvolt to ten million electronvolts, each division ten times the previous one. The energy of visible-light photons is 1.7–3.3 electronvolts. The vertical dashed line at 12.6 electronvolts is the ionisation energy of water: photons with a greater energy are ionising, and that region is shaded. In the ionising region an X-ray photon of 60 kiloelectronvolts and a gamma photon of caesium-137 of 662 kiloelectronvolts are marked.
Kaavakuva, ei mittakaavassa: kolme vaaka: Schematic figure, not to scale: three horizontal tissue bands in which cells lie side by side. In the top band an alpha particle travels only a distance of a few cells and stops, and its track is full of ion pairs densely next to each other. In the middle band a beta particle, that is an electron, travels in a winding path through the whole band, and its track has ion pairs only sparsely. In the bottom band a gamma photon travels straight through the band and interacts only once: it removes an electron, which ionises a few molecules over a short distance. An ion pair is drawn as a red positive ion and a blue electron.
Kaavakuva, ei mittakaavassa: vasemmalla: Schematic figure, not to scale: on the left a radiation source from which three rays go to the right. Violet alpha radiation stops at the first barrier, a sheet of paper 0.1 millimetres thick. Blue beta radiation passes through the paper but stops at the second barrier, a 5 millimetre aluminium plate. Orange wavy gamma radiation passes through the paper and the aluminium and is weakened in a 5 centimetre layer of lead; after the lead it is drawn thinner, because only a small part of it gets through.
Kaavakuva, ei mittakaavassa: Geigerin ja: Schematic figure, not to scale: a Geiger–Müller tube cut lengthwise. The tube is a metal cylinder filled with a noble gas. At the left end there is a thin window, and a thin metal wire runs through the middle. The wire is at a positive and the wall at a negative voltage, about 500 volts. A blue beta particle comes in through the window and removes an electron from a gas atom. The electron accelerates towards the wire and removes new electrons on its way, so an electron avalanche forms near the wire. The avalanche shows up as a current pulse, which the counter counts.
Kuvaaja mittakaavassa: läpi päässeen gam: Graph to scale: the fraction I over I zero of the gamma radiation that has got through as a function of the barrier thickness d, thickness from zero to 25 millimetres. Gamma radiation of caesium-137, narrow beam. In lead the fraction halves after every 5.5 millimetre layer: a half at 5.5 millimetres, a quarter at 11 millimetres and an eighth at 16.5 millimetres. In aluminium the fraction falls slowly and is about 0.6 at 25 millimetres.
Kuvaaja mittakaavassa: gammasäteilyn net: Graph to scale: the net pulse rate of gamma radiation in pulses per minute behind plates of an unknown material as a function of the total thickness d of the plates, thickness from zero to 48 millimetres, grid spacing 2 millimetres and 50 pulses per minute. Without plates the pulse rate is 800 pulses per minute, and the curve falls ever more gently.
